metadata.title: The One Step No Script Can Skip.
metadata.subtitle: The m5-onboard Skill (Claude Code Plugins)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: when a Claude Code skill automates flashing and provisioning a physical device end to end, does 'one command' mean the whole thing runs hands-off? Lands the carry-out that automation covers every stage but one — the button press stays a human's job, and no flag replaces it.

beats.narration_text: Someone assumed one script flashes this board with zero exceptions. It doesn't — the button dance is the one exception, done by hand. So: flash my board with one script — one exception?

beats.narration_text: The whole workflow runs through one command: onboard.py --apps buddy. Underneath, that's four stages. Detect finds the board over USB — the port name differs by system, usbmodem on macOS, ttyACM or ttyUSB on Linux, COM on Windows — then confirms the actual chip. Identify checks hardware signatures for a likely firmware match, but the final choice is always stated explicitly, never guessed. Flash writes the firmware itself. Install copies the real program files onto the board and restarts it. Two smaller tools exist for narrower jobs: pushing just the app bundle to a board that's already flashed, or running a hardware check afterward.

Three things matter once you're actually running this. First: two boards share the exact same USB signature, so the script can't tell them apart on its own — guess the variant wrong and the device boot-loops. Second: a full run takes two to three minutes, so it goes in the background with its output streamed to a log file; a silent terminal for three minutes looks exactly like a crash. Third, the flash step itself: on boards that connect over native USB, there's no software line the script can pulse to reset the chip into flashing mode — so it's a physical dance. Hold one button, tap reset while still holding it, hold one more second, then let go. The script waits for a person to actually do that.

production_viz.label: THE BUTTON DANCE
production_viz.caption: the one step that needs a hand

beats.narration_text: That physical step isn't universal. It's needed only because native-USB boards have no control line the script can pulse to force a reset — the standard software trick, toggling two control lines, is simply a no-op there. Boards that connect through a separate USB-to-serial bridge chip skip the button dance entirely: that same software trick works normally, and the whole flash step runs through without anyone touching the board. Same script, same command — which path it takes depends entirely on which USB hardware happens to be inside.
One script can detect, identify, flash, and install this board — every stage but one. The button press stays a human's job. No flag replaces a thumb.

Then watch: does Claude name the button dance before it starts, or does it just launch the script and wait?
